title: Deep Double Descent
hook: Bigger models should overfit, then get worse — right? Instead test error often dips, climbs, then dips again as model size grows, breaking the classic bias-variance story.
key_points: Test error follows a double-descent curve: it worsens, then improves again as model size grows.
A similar pattern appears over training time, called epoch-wise double descent.
Introduces 'effective model complexity' as a unifying measure behind the effect.
In some regimes, adding more training data — even 4x — can hurt test performance.
content_html: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Yamini Bansal, and colleagues showed that the textbook picture — where error keeps rising once a model is big enough to overfit — is incomplete. They document a "double descent" curve where test error first worsens, then improves again as models grow larger. They also find the same shape unfolding over training time, an effect they call epoch-wise double descent.
extra_html:
What it is

The authors unify these observations under a single notion they call "effective model complexity," and propose a generalized double-descent conjecture to describe when the second descent kicks in. Strikingly, they identify regimes where adding more training data — even quadrupling it — can actually hurt test performance rather than help.

Why it matters

The result complicates the classic bias-variance tradeoff, which predicts a single sweet spot of model size beyond which things only get worse. By showing that error can recover past the interpolation point, the paper helps explain why very large, overparametrized networks generalize well in practice.

related.title: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
related.hook: Too simple and your model misses the pattern; too flexible and it chases noise. Generalization lives between the two.

related.title: Overfitting & Regularization
related.hook: A model that aces its training data but flops on anything new hasn't learned — it has memorized. Regularization is the cure.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

flashcards.back_html: It worsens, then improves again — a double-descent curve — rather than just rising once the model is big enough to overfit.
